note_claims.claim: The patient presents with right-sided sciatica-type leg pain for three weeks.
The onset of pain occurred three weeks ago while lifting a resident at work.
Pain radiates from the buttock down the posterior thigh and lateral calf into the foot.
The patient reports pain is worse than back pain.
Pain severity is up to 7/10 and is worse after sitting.
The patient experiences occasional tingling over the lateral foot.
The patient denies weakness.
The patient denies saddle anaesthesia or change in bladder or bowel function.
The patient denies fevers.
The patient has no history of cancer or unintentional weight loss.
The patient takes over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with little benefit.
The patient has no known drug allergies.
The patient has no history of peptic ulcer, asthma, or renal disease.
Lumbar flexion is limited by pain.
Straight leg raise is positive on the right at 40 degrees and negative on the left.
Power, reflexes, and sensation are normal and symmetrical in both lower limbs.
The impression is right-sided sciatica, likely lumbar disc-related radiculopathy, with no red flags.
The plan is to switch the patient from ibuprofen to naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food and add omeprazole 20 mg once daily for two weeks.
The patient is referred to physiotherapy.
The patient is advised to keep active and avoid bed rest.
A fit note for two weeks is issued, allowing the patient to be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling).
A follow-up appointment is scheduled in four weeks.
The patient is advised to attend A&E immediately if they experience saddle numbness, difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or bilateral leg weakness (cauda equina symptoms).

transcript_facts.fact: Patient reports experiencing shooting pain going all the way down their leg.
Pain started about three weeks ago while lifting a resident at work.
Patient works as a care assistant at a nursing home.
Patient initially stated the pain was in the left leg, but corrected themselves to the right leg.
The pain radiates from the bum, down the back of the thigh, round the outside of the calf, and into the foot.
Pain is rated seven out of ten on a bad day and is worse when sitting for a while.
Patient confirms the pain is definitely in the leg, not the back.
Patient reports a bit of tingling on the outside of their foot sometimes.
Patient denies any weakness, stating it is just painful.
Patient denies numbness around their bottom or between their legs when sitting on the toilet.
Patient denies any change in waterworks (trouble passing urine or leaking).
Patient denies any problems with bowels or accidents.
Patient denies any fevers or feeling unwell.
Patient denies having ever had cancer or lost weight without trying.
Patient was taking Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day, which they felt 'barely touches it'.
Patient states they have no other medicines and no allergies.
Clinician asked the patient to bend forward and lift the right leg up straight to check for pain.
Patient reported pain shooting down when the leg was lifted.
Clinician noted the pain was at about 40 degrees when the leg was lifted.
Patient confirmed the left leg was fine when tested.
Clinician noted that power, knee and ankle reflexes were normal in both legs.
Patient confirmed they could feel the clinician touching both sides of their legs.
Clinician suggested the findings sound like sciatica, where a disc in the lower back is irritating a nerve going down the right leg.
Clinician decided to switch the patient's medication from ibuprofen to naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food and add omeprazole 20 mg once a day.
Clinician referred the patient to physiotherapy.
Clinician provided a fit note for two weeks, stating the patient may be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling).
Clinician scheduled a review appointment in four weeks.

Clinician provided safety-netting advice to attend A&E immediately if the patient experiences saddle numbness, difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or bilateral leg weakness (cauda equina symptoms).
